title: A hymn in Basant
hook: Ramanand sets out for the temple with sandalwood, and is turned back toward his own heart

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Basant, the raga of spring, and Guru Nanak's month in which spring is always present. Your line was spring. What did you find quietly growing? Day one thousand one hundred fifteen.

Sandalwood, ground into a paste on a stone. Fragrant oils in small bottles. A man gathers them up one day, the way you'd gather what you need for something important, and sets out to worship God in a temple. He has everything ready. He knows the way. And somewhere between his door and the temple, his plan changes. The man is the Bhagat Ramanand, and he tells the story himself, in a hymn the Gurus placed in the Basant section of the Guru Granth Sahib. Today: where he was going, and where he ended up.
screen: `SANDALWOOD AND FRAGRANT OILS.` → `HE SETS OUT FOR THE TEMPLE.` → `THE PLAN CHANGES.`

segments.voice: The hymn begins at the end of the story, with a question. In paraphrase: where should I go? My own home has been colored with joy. My mind no longer wanders; it has gone still. Then he tells us how. One day, a longing rose in him. He ground sandalwood with fragrant oils and set out to worship God in the temple. But that God, he says, the Guru showed him inside his own heart. Wherever he went after that, he found the One already there, present in everything. The hymn ends with thanks: he offers himself to the true Guru, who cut away his confusion and doubt, and he names his Lord as the One who pervades all. Tradition remembers Ramanand as a teacher whom other Bhagats looked to, and links Kabir with him; the hymn itself says nothing about that, so hold it as tradition. What the hymn does say is the turn from going to staying. The sandalwood isn't mocked. The longing that sent him out the door is real, and the hymn honors it as the start of the story. But the finding happens at home. And the word for what happens to his home is a color word, rang, the same word used for dye and for love. His house is dyed with it. Now set that inside Basant, the raga of spring. Yesterday the Granth spoke of a spring that is always present. Today Ramanand shows where it was all along. Not out on the road. In the house, in the heart. Your line: spring at home.
screen: `WHERE SHOULD I GO?` · `MY HOME IS COLORED WITH JOY.` · `SHOWN GOD IN HIS OWN HEART.` · `THE FINDING HAPPENS AT HOME.` · then, large: `SPRING AT HOME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to one Basant shabad, and stay where you are. If you can, play Ramanand's hymn or another shabad sung in Basant. If not, sit in the quiet. Notice the room around you, exactly as it is: the light, the sounds, the slightly untidy corner. Resist the small urge to be somewhere better. Then bring your attention inward, to the breath, and rest there as if you've just come home after a long trip. If you pray, you can remember the One the hymn says is already present. If you don't, simply let this room be enough for now. The bell holds the time.
A hymn in Basant. Ramanand's song of setting out with sandalwood to worship, and being shown God in his own heart, so that his home is colored with joy. Today's word.

Your line: spring at home. Once today, when you catch yourself wishing to be elsewhere, look up at the place you're actually in and find one thing worth staying for. Day one thousand one hundred fifteen.

howItsDone: Ramanand's hymn is sung in kirtan in Raga Basant, alongside the Gurus' own hymns; Sikhs honor the Bhagats whose words the Gurus placed in the Guru Granth Sahib.

original.note: rang: color, dye, and love; Ramanand's home is colored with it.

trapdoor: what you thought: to find God you go somewhere holy.
what it means: Ramanand set out to worship and was shown the One in his own heart.
what a scholar hears: the hymn tells the story backward, opening with 'where should I go?', and its word for joy at home is rang, color and love at once.
